Abstract

Thermodynamic quantities of Coulomb plasmas consisting of point-like ions immersed in a compressible, polarizable electron background are calculated for ion charges Z=Z= 1 to 26 and for a wide domain of plasma parameters ranging from the Debye-Hückel limit to the crystallization point and from the region of nondegenerate to fully degenerate nonrelativistic or relativistic electrons. The calculations are based on the linear-response theory for the electron-ion interaction, including the local-field corrections in the electronic dielectric function. The thermodynamic quantities are calculated in the framework of the NN-body hypernetted-chain equations and fitted by analytic expressions. We present also accurate analytic approximations for the free energy of the ideal electron gas at arbitrary degeneracy and relativity and for the excess free energy of the one-component plasma of ions (OCP) derived from Monte Carlo simulations. The extension to multi-ionic mixtures is discussed within the framework of the linear mixing rule. These formulae provide a completely analytic, accurate description of the thermodynamic quantities of fully ionized electron-ion Coulomb plasmas, a useful tool for various applications from liquid state theory to dense stellar matter.

I Introduction

Electron-ion plasmas (EIP) consisting of different species of point-like ions (charge Zi​eZ_{i}e, mass mi=Aim_{i}=A_{i} a.m.u.) and electrons (−e-e, mem_{e}) are encountered in numerous physical and astrophysical situations like, e.g., inertially confined laboratory plasmas, liquid metals, stellar and planetary interiors, supernova explosions, etc. [1]. Full ionization is reached either at high temperatures TT and low densities ρ\rho (thermal ionization) or at high enough densities ρ\rho (pressure ionization). Even when these conditions are not satisfied, the approximation of full ionization is useful for calculations in the mean-ion approximation, in which the mean ion charge corresponds to its partial ionization stage. On the other hand, the free energy of fully ionized EIP provides the reference system for models aimed at describing the thermodynamic properties of partially ionized plasmas [2]. In this paper, we present a completely analytic model for the free energy of EIP, based on detailed numerical calculations for different ionic species ZZ over a wide range of density and temperature. We first focus on the two-component plasma (TCP), consisting of electrons and a single species of ions. Extension to ionic mixtures is considered in Sect. VI.

The Coulomb plasmas can be characterized by the electron coupling parameter Γe\Gamma_{e} and the density parameter rsr_{s},

Γe=β​e2/ae,rs=ae/aB,\Gamma_{e}=\beta e^{2}/a_{e},\qquad r_{s}=a_{e}/a_{B}, (1)

where β=(kB​T)−1\beta=(k_{B}T)^{-1} is the inverse thermodynamic temperature, kBk_{B} is the Boltzmann constant, ae=(43πne)−1/3a_{e}=(\frac{4}{3}\pi n_{e})^{-1/3} measures the mean inter-electron distance, nen_{e} is the electron number density, and aB=ℏ2/(me​e2)a_{B}=\hbar^{2}/(m_{e}e^{2}) is the Bohr radius. These parameters can be evaluated as Γe≈(2.693×105​K/T)​n241/3=(23.2​eV/kB​T)​n241/3\Gamma_{e}\approx(2.693\times 10^{5}\,\mbox{K}/T)\,n_{24}^{1/3}=(23.2\,\mbox{eV}/k_{B}T)\,n_{24}^{1/3} and rs≈1.172n24−1/3,r_{s}\approx 1.172\,n_{24}^{-1/3}, where n24≡ne/1024n_{24}\equiv n_{e}/10^{24} cm≈−3(ρ/1.6605gcm−3)⟨Z⟩/⟨A⟩{}^{-3}\approx(\rho/1.6605{\rm~g~cm}^{-3})\langle Z\rangle/\langle A\rangle. Here and hereafter, ⟨X⟩=∑ini​Xi/∑ini\langle X\rangle=\sum_{i}n_{i}X_{i}\,/\sum_{i}n_{i} denotes the average over all ions and nin_{i} the number density of ions of iith species.

The ion coupling parameter of the TCP is

Γi=β​(Z​e)2/ai=Γe​Z5/3,\Gamma_{i}=\beta\,(Ze)^{2}/a_{i}=\Gamma_{e}\,Z^{5/3}, (2)

where aia_{i} is the mean interionic distance (ai=ae​Z1/3a_{i}=a_{e}Z^{1/3} due to the electroneutrality condition ne=ni​Zn_{e}=n_{i}Z). In multicomponent plasmas (MCP), it may be useful to define Γi=Γe​⟨Z5/3⟩.\Gamma_{i}=\Gamma_{e}\langle Z^{5/3}\rangle.

The degeneracy parameter θ\theta and the relativity parameter xx are defined respectively as:

θ=T/TF,x=pF/(me​c),\theta=T/T_{F},\qquad x=p_{F}/(m_{e}c), (3)

where TF=(me​c2/kB)​[1+x2−1]≈(5.93×109​K)​[1+x2−1]T_{F}=(m_{e}c^{2}/k_{B})\,[\sqrt{1+x^{2}}-1]\approx(5.93\times 10^{9}\,\mbox{K})\,[\sqrt{1+x^{2}}-1] is the Fermi temperature, cc is the speed of light, and pF=ℏ​(3​π2​ne)1/3p_{F}=\hbar(3\pi^{2}n_{e})^{1/3} is the zero-temperature Fermi momentum of electrons. To estimate θ\theta and xx, it is useful to note that

x=(9​π4)1/3​αrs≈0.014rs≈(⟨Z⟩⟨A⟩​ρ106​ g cm−3)1/3,\displaystyle x=\left({9\pi\over 4}\right)^{1/3}{\alpha\over r_{s}}\approx{0.014\over r_{s}}\approx\left({\langle Z\rangle\over\langle A\rangle}{\rho\over 10^{6}\mbox{~g~cm}^{-3}}\right)^{1/3}, (4)
θ=α2​(Γe​rs)−11+x2−1,θ≈0.543​rsΓeat ​x≪1,\displaystyle\theta={\alpha^{2}(\Gamma_{e}r_{s})^{-1}\over\sqrt{1+x^{2}}-1},\quad\theta\approx 0.543\,{r_{s}\over\Gamma_{e}}\quad\mbox{at~}x\ll 1, (5)

where α=1/137.036\alpha=1/137.036 is the fine-structure constant.

Various asymptotic expansions, interpolation formulae and large tables have been derived over the past for the thermodynamic functions of free fermions (see Refs.[3, 4] and references therein). In this paper, we present analytic expressions for the thermodynamic quantities of free fermions for arbitrary degeneracy and relativity, θ\theta and xx. Secondly, we propose simple and accurate analytic approximations for the nonideal internal and free energies of the classical one-component plasma (OCP), which take into account the most recent hypernetted-chain (HNC) and Monte Carlo (MC) calculations by DeWitt et al.[5] (DWSC) in the strong-coupling regime. Third, we consider the electron screening effects on the thermodynamic properties of the TCP. We employ a computational HNC scheme based on the linear screening theory with local field corrections, taking into account the finite temperature (finite θ\theta) effects. The numerical calculations have been performed over a wide range of ZZ, Γi\Gamma_{i}, and rsr_{s}, and interpolated by a simple analytic formula, which recovers the Debye-Hückel (DH) limit for the TCP at Γi≪1\Gamma_{i}\ll 1 and the Thomas-Fermi limit at large Γi\Gamma_{i} and ZZ.

II Summary of the model

Consider the Helmholtz free energy FF, internal energy UU, and pressure PP of a TCP of NiN_{i} ions and NeN_{e} electrons in the volume VV. The total free energy FtotF_{\rm tot} can be written as the sum of three terms,

Ftot=Fid(i)+Fid(e)+Fex,F_{\rm tot}=F_{\rm id}^{(i)}+F_{\rm id}^{(e)}+F_{\rm ex}, (6)

where Fid(i,e)F_{\rm id}^{(i,e)} denote the ideal free energy of ions and electrons, respectively, and FexF_{\rm ex} is the excess free energy arising from interactions.

In this paper, we restrict ourselves to conditions where the ions behave classically, which is the case in most astrophysical situations. Quantum corrections for ions which can be important in the ultradense matter of white dwarf interiors, neutron stars, and supernova cores have been considered, e.g., in Refs.[6, 7]. Thus Fid(i)F_{\rm id}^{(i)} is given by the Maxwell-Boltzmann expression. For Fid(e)F_{\rm id}^{(e)}, we use the well-known expressions of the thermodynamic functions of the perfect gas of fermions (which may be degenerate and relativistic) through the generalized Fermi-Dirac integrals.

To calculate FexF_{\rm ex}, we follow the model developed by Chabrier [8] for fully ionized EIPs. As long as the ion-electron interaction is weak compared to the kinetic energy of the electrons, Z​e2/ae≪kB​TFZe^{2}/a_{e}\ll k_{B}T_{F}, this interaction can be treated within the linear screening theory. Under these conditions, the exact Hamiltonian of the TCP can be separated out exactly into a Hamiltonian for the electron-screened ionic fluid and a Hamiltonian for a rigid electron background, the so-called “jellium” Hamiltonian HeH_{e} [9, 10]:

H=Heff+HeH=H^{\rm eff}\,+\,H_{e} (7)

with

Heff=Ki+12​V​∑𝐤≠04​π​(Z​e)2k2​[ρ𝐤​ρ𝐤∗ϵ⁡(k)−Ni]H^{\rm eff}=K_{i}\,+\,\frac{1}{2V}\sum_{{\bf k}\neq 0}\frac{4\pi(Ze)^{2}}{k^{2}}\left[\frac{\rho_{\bf k}\rho_{\bf k}^{\ast}}{\epsilon(k)}-N_{i}\right] (8)

where KiK_{i} is the ionic kinetic (translational) term, ρ𝐤\rho_{\bf k} is the Fourier component of the ionic microscopic density and ϵ⁡(k)\epsilon(k) is the static screening function of the electron fluid to be discussed below. The Hamiltonian HeffH^{\rm eff} characterizes the electron-screened ion fluid with the interparticle potential whose Fourier transform is

Veff​(k)=4​π​(Z​e)2k2​ϵ​(k),V^{\rm eff}(k)=\frac{4\pi(Ze)^{2}}{k^{2}\epsilon(k)}, (9)

which is the sum of the bare ionic potential and the induced polarization potential.

The ion-ion (i​iii) and the ion-electron (i​eie) Coulomb interactions can thus be separated from the exchange-correlation contribution in the electron fluid (e​eee). The excess part of the free energy (6) can then be written as Fex=Fe​e+Fi​i+Fi​eF_{\rm ex}=F_{ee}+F_{ii}+F_{ie}; the quantities labeled i​eie will be referred to as electron-screening quantities. It is convenient to consider dimensionless quantities fe​e≡β​Fe​e/Nef_{ee}\equiv\beta F_{ee}/N_{e} and fi​i,i​e≡β​Fi​i,i​e/Nif_{ii,ie}\equiv\beta F_{ii,ie}/N_{i}. Then

fex=xe​fe​e+xi​(fi​i+fi​e),f_{\rm ex}=x_{e}f_{ee}+x_{i}(f_{ii}+f_{ie}), (10)

where xi,e≡Ni,e/Nx_{i,e}\equiv N_{i,e}/N denote the number fraction of ions and electrons, respectively, and N=Ni+NeN=N_{i}+N_{e} is the total number of particles. In the same way we define ue​e≡β​Ue​e/Neu_{ee}\equiv\beta U_{ee}/N_{e} and ui​i,i​e≡β​Ui​i,i​e/Niu_{ii,ie}\equiv\beta U_{ii,ie}/N_{i}. The excess free energy can be obtained from the internal energy by integration:

fex​(Γ,rs)=∫0Γuex​(Γ,rs)Γ​𝑑Γ.f_{\rm ex}(\Gamma,r_{s})=\int_{0}^{\Gamma}{u_{\rm ex}(\Gamma,r_{s})\over\Gamma}\,{\rm d}\Gamma. (11)

For fe​ef_{ee}, we have adopted the interpolation formula of Ichimaru et al.[11] (hereafter IIT), consistent with numerical results obtained by different authors.

For fi​if_{ii}, which corresponds to the well-known OCP model, that implies the rigid electron background (ϵ⁡(k)=1\epsilon(k)=1), we present an analytic interpolation between the MC results [5] at Γi≥1\Gamma_{i}\geq 1 and the DH limit and Abe correction at Γi≲0.1\Gamma_{i}\lesssim 0.1.

The ion-electron interactions are calculated numerically as in Ref.[8]. In this approach, the bare Coulomb potential in the expression for the electrostatic energy is replaced by the potential statistically screened by the electrons (9), and the HNC approximation is used to calculate the thermodynamic functions of the system. This model, originally applied to nonrelativistic hydrogen plasmas, is now extended to the case of arbitrary ZZ and xx. In the nonrelativistic case (x≪1x\ll 1), the dielectric function ϵ⁡(k)\epsilon(k) is the finite-temperature Lindhard function modified with the local field correction arising from electron correlation effects.

At very high density, x≳1x\gtrsim 1, the electrons become relativistic. At such densities, the electron correlation effects are completely negligible. The finite-temperature effects (θ≠0\theta\neq 0) may give an appreciable contribution to the screening part of the free energy fi​ef_{ie} only at extremely high temperatures, where the nonideality of the gas has no significance. Thus we use the Jancovici [12] zero-temperature dielectric function in the relativistic regime.

The correlation functions and thermodynamic quantities for the electron-screened ionic fluid are obtained within the framework of the HNC equations. The validity of the HNC theory for the Coulomb systems has been assessed by several authors by comparison with lengthy MC simulations. The HNC approximation consists of neglecting the contribution of the so-called bridge diagrams, which involves an infinite series of multiple integrals, in the NN-body general diagrammatic resummations [13]. The long-range part of the direct correlation function c⁡(r)c(r) calculated within the HNC approximation is exactly canceled by −V(r)/kT-V(r)/kT, so that the pair correlation function g⁡(r)g(r) is of much shorter range than the Coulomb potential V⁡(r)V(r) [13]. This is a required condition for Coulomb systems, because of the perfect screening condition. This property of the HNC theory makes it particularly suitable for such long-range systems. The differences on the free energy, the internal energy and the pressure are at most of the order of 1% (see, e.g., Refs.[5, 8]). The difference is due to the lack of bridge functions in the HNC theory.

III Ideal part of the free energy

The ideal free energy of nonrelativistic classical ions, neglecting their spin statistics, reads[14]:

Fid(i)=Ni​kB​T​[ln⁡(ni​λi3)−1],F_{\rm id}^{(i)}=N_{i}k_{B}T\left[\ln(n_{i}\lambda_{i}^{3})-1\right], (12)

where λi=(2​π​β​ℏ2/mi)1/2\lambda_{i}=(2\pi\beta\hbar^{2}/m_{i})^{1/2} is the thermal wavelength of ions. For electrons, we use the identity[14]

Fid(e)=Ne​μid(e)−Pid(e)​V.F_{\rm id}^{(e)}=N_{e}\mu_{\rm id}^{(e)}-P_{\rm id}^{(e)}V. (13)

Here, μid(e)\mu_{\rm id}^{(e)} is the chemical potential (in which we do not include the rest energy me​c2m_{e}c^{2}) and Pid(e)P_{\rm id}^{(e)} is the pressure of the ideal Fermi gas. The pressure and number density, in turn, are functions of μ\mu and TT:

Pid(e)\displaystyle P_{\rm id}^{(e)} =\displaystyle= (2​me)3/23​π2​ℏ3​β5/2​(I3/2​(χ,τ)+τ2​I5/2​(χ,τ)),\displaystyle{(2m_{e})^{3/2}\over 3\pi^{2}\hbar^{3}\beta^{5/2}}\left(I_{3/2}(\chi,\tau)+{\tau\over 2}I_{5/2}(\chi,\tau)\right), (14)
ne\displaystyle n_{e} =\displaystyle= 2​(me/β)3/2π2​ℏ3​(I1/2​(χ,τ)+τ​I3/2​(χ,τ)),\displaystyle{\sqrt{2}\,(m_{e}/\beta)^{3/2}\over\pi^{2}\hbar^{3}}\left(I_{1/2}(\chi,\tau)+\tau I_{3/2}(\chi,\tau)\right), (15)

where τ=(β​me​c2)−1=T/5.93×109\tau=(\beta m_{e}c^{2})^{-1}=T/5.93\times 10^{9} K, χ=β​μid(e)\chi=\beta\mu_{\rm id}^{(e)}, and

Iν​(χ,τ)≡∫0∞xν​1+τ​x/2exp⁡(x−χ)+1​𝑑xI_{\nu}(\chi,\tau)\equiv\int_{0}^{\infty}{x^{\nu}\,\sqrt{1+\tau x/2}\over\exp(x-\chi)+1}{\rm d}x (16)

is the generalized Fermi-Dirac integral.

In the limit τ→0\tau\to 0, the Fermi-Dirac integrals reduce to the usual nonrelativistic Fermi integrals Iν​(χ)I_{\nu}(\chi), which can be calculated using the highly accurate Padé approximations presented by Antia [15]. The chemical potential is obtained from the relationship

χ=X1/2(2θ−3/2/3),\chi=X_{1/2}(2\theta^{-3/2}/3), (17)

where XνX_{\nu} is the inverse Fermi integral, also fitted with high accuracy by Antia [15].

The accuracy of the nonrelativistic formulae decreases rapidly at T>107T>10^{7} K. Blinnikov et al.[3] have presented a number of approximations and asymptotic expansions of the relativistic thermodynamic functions of the ideal electron gas. We have selected those of their fitting formulae that are most accurate at low and moderate χ\chi and supplemented them with asymptotic expansions at high χ\chi to obtain an approximation which is accurate at any nen_{e} for each of the Fermi integrals Iν​(χ,τ)I_{\nu}(\chi,\tau) with ν=12,32\nu=\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}, and 52\frac{5}{2} :

where R≡χ⁡(1+χ​τ/2)R\equiv\sqrt{\chi(1+\chi\tau/2)},

If χ​τ≪1\chi\tau\ll 1, the functions Fk​(χ,τ)F_{k}(\chi,\tau) should be replaced by their nonrelativistic limits, χk+3/2/(k+3/2)\chi^{k+3/2}/(k+3/2). The constants ci(k)c_{i}^{(k)}, χi(k)\chi_{i}^{(k)}, xix_{i}, ξi\xi_{i}, hih_{i}, and viv_{i} are adopted from Ref.[3] and listed in Table 1. The relative error of the approximation (18)–(20) does not exceed 0.2% at τ≤102\tau\leq 10^{2} (any χ\chi), being typically a few parts in 10410^{4}.

The chemical potential μid(e)\mu_{\rm id}^{(e)} can be obtained numerically from Eq. (15), using Eqs. (18)–(20). We have constructed also an analytic fit to χ\chi:

χ=χnonrel−32​ln⁡[1+(τ1+τ/(2​θ))​1+q1​τ+q2​q3​τ1+q2​τ].\chi=\chi^{\rm nonrel}-{3\over 2}\ln\left[1+\left({\tau\over 1+\tau/(2\theta)}\right){1+q_{1}\,\sqrt{\tau}+q_{2}q_{3}\tau\over 1+q_{2}\tau}\right]. (24)

Here χnonrel\chi^{\rm nonrel} is given by the nonrelativistic formula (17), and the coefficients qiq_{i} are functions of θ\theta:

q1\displaystyle q_{1} =\displaystyle= 32​(eθ−1)−1,\displaystyle\frac{3}{2}({\rm e}^{\theta}-1)^{-1},
q2\displaystyle q_{2} =\displaystyle= 12+8θ−3/2,\displaystyle 12+8\theta^{-3/2},
q3\displaystyle q_{3} =\displaystyle= 2π1/3−e−θ+1.612​eθ6.192​θ0.0944​e−θ+5.535​θ0.698​eθ.\displaystyle{2\over\pi^{1/3}}-{{\rm\,e}^{-\theta}+1.612{\rm\,e}^{\theta}\over 6.192\,\theta^{0.0944}{\rm\,e}^{-\theta}+5.535\,\theta^{0.698}{\rm\,e}^{\theta}}.

The relative error δ​χ/χ\delta\chi/\chi becomes infinite at χ=0\chi=0. However, since thermodynamic quantities are expressed through χ\chi by virtue of thermal averaging of type of Eq. (16), a natural measure of the error is δ​χ/max⁡(|χ|,1)=δ​μ/max⁡(|μ|,kB​T)\delta\chi/\max(|\chi|,1)=\delta\mu/\max(|\mu|,k_{B}T). The error thus lies within 0.4% for τ>1\tau>1 and is smaller than 0.2% if τ<1\tau<1 (any θ\theta). Another measure of the accuracy is the relative difference between the densities nen_{e} calculated with the exact and fitted values of μ\mu. This difference lies within 0.4% for τ≥1\tau\geq 1 and within 0.1% for τ<1\tau<1.

This accuracy may not be sufficient for calculation of temperature derivatives of the electron-gas EOS (heat capacity, temperature exponent, etc.) in the regime of strong degeneracy (χ≫1\chi\gg 1). In this case, however, Sommerfeld asymptotic expansions for these quantities may be used (see, e.g., Ref.[16]).

In this paper we do not consider the positrons, which are efficiently created at τ≳1\tau\gtrsim 1 (see Ref.[3] for description of the equilibrium electron-positron plasma).

IV OCP liquid of classical ions

Liquid and solid phases of the OCP have been studied extensively by various numerical methods, MC simulations or NN-body semianalytic theories like the HNC theory (see Refs. [17, 11] for detailed reviews). All the thermodynamic functions of the OCP of classical ions in a uniform (rigid) electron background can be expressed as functions of the only parameter Γi\Gamma_{i}. The melting point of the OCP corresponds to Γi≈172\Gamma_{i}\approx 172, above which it forms a Coulomb crystal[18]. The most accurate MC and HNC results for the internal and free energies of the liquid OCP for 1≤Γi≤1601\leq\Gamma_{i}\leq 160 have been obtained recently by DWSC [5] (see references therein for earlier results). The high precision of the calculations allowed the authors to investigate the tiny effects of nonadditivity of the excess energy of binary ionic mixtures, as will be commented in Sect. VI.

DWSC have also derived a highly accurate analytic fit to the MC simulations of the internal energy of the OCP in the aforementioned Γ\Gamma-range:

ui​i=a​Γi+b​Γis+c,u_{ii}=a\Gamma_{i}+b\Gamma_{i}^{s}+c, (25)

with a=−0.899126a=-0.899126, b=0.60712b=0.60712, c=−0.27998c=-0.27998, and s=0.321308s=0.321308. The maximum relative difference between calculated and fitted values reaches 17 parts in 10510^{5} at Γi=3.1748\Gamma_{i}=3.1748.

Equation (25), however, does not apply to the weak-coupling region Γi<1\Gamma_{i}<1. At very small Γi\Gamma_{i}, the internal energy of the OCP must recover the well-known DH expression ui​i=−(3/2)​Γi3/2u_{ii}=-(\sqrt{3}/2)\,\Gamma_{i}^{3/2} whereas at moderately small Γi\Gamma_{i} this limit must include the Abe correction [19]:

ui​i=−32​Γi3/2−3​Γi3​[38​ln⁡(3​Γi)+γ2−13],u_{ii}=-{\sqrt{3}\over 2}\,\Gamma_{i}^{3/2}-3\Gamma_{i}^{3}\,\left[\frac{3}{8}\ln(3\Gamma_{i})+{\gamma\over 2}-\frac{1}{3}\right], (26)

where γ=0.57721​…\gamma=0.57721\ldots is the Euler’s constant.

We represent the internal energy of the ionic fluid (Γi≲170\Gamma_{i}\lesssim 170) by a simplified version of the fitting formula proposed by Hansen[20, 21],

ui​i=Γi3/2​[A1A2+Γi+A31+Γi],u_{ii}=\Gamma_{i}^{3/2}\left[{A_{1}\over\sqrt{A_{2}+\Gamma_{i}}}+{A_{3}\over 1+\Gamma_{i}}\right], (27)

where A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} are fitting parameters, and A3=−3/2−A1/A2A_{3}=-\sqrt{3}/2-A_{1}/\sqrt{A_{2}}. We have found that the minimum relative difference between Eq. (27) and the MC results of DWSC[5] — smaller than 6 parts in 10410^{4} — is obtained with A1=−0.9052A_{1}=-0.9052 and A2=0.6322A_{2}=0.6322. This accuracy is sufficient for our present study since it is much better than the available numerical accuracy of the complementary contribution to the internal energy, ui​eu_{ie}. As mentioned in Sect. II, the HNC calculations of the sum ui​i+ui​eu_{ii}+u_{ie} ensure an accuracy of the order of 1%.

Figure 1 presents a comparison of our interpolation formula (27) with the DH-Abe formulae, the MC results and fit (25) of DWSC[5], and the interpolation proposed by Stolzmann and Blöcker [22] (hereafter SB) following Ebeling [23]. Unlike SB, our Eq. (27) accurately reproduces Eq. (26) in the range Γi∼0.01−0.1\Gamma_{i}\sim 0.01-0.1 and provides a smoother transition between the strong- (Γi>1\Gamma_{i}>1) and weak- (Γi≪1\Gamma_{i}\ll 1) coupling regimes.

Using Eqs. (27) and (11) we obtain the Helmholtz free energy (cf. Ref.[20]):

fi​i​(Γi)\displaystyle f_{ii}(\Gamma_{i}) =\displaystyle= A1​[Γi​(A2+Γi)−A2​ln⁡(Γi/A2+1+Γi/A2)]\displaystyle A_{1}\left[\sqrt{\Gamma_{i}(A_{2}+\Gamma_{i})}-A_{2}\,\ln\left(\sqrt{\Gamma_{i}/A_{2}}+\sqrt{1+\Gamma_{i}/A_{2}}\right)\right] (28)
+2​A3​[Γi−arctan⁡(Γi)].\displaystyle+2A_{3}\left[\sqrt{\Gamma_{i}}-\arctan\left(\sqrt{\Gamma_{i}}\right)\right].

At Γi≥1\Gamma_{i}\geq 1, this formula gives fi​if_{ii} which differs from the HNC calculations and fit of DWSC[5] by no more than 0.8%. This difference approximately coincides with that between the MC and HNC results for ui​iu_{ii}, therefore it should be attributed to the lack of the bridge functions in the HNC approximation (see Sect. II). On the other hand, Eq. (28) recovers the DH-Abe free energy with an error smaller than 0.6% at Γi<0.1\Gamma_{i}<0.1.

V Electron fluid

The exchange and correlation effects in electron fluid were studied by many authors. For instance, Tanaka et al.[24] calculated the interaction energy of the electron fluid at finite temperature in the Singwi-Tosi-Land-Sjölander [25] approximation and presented a fitting formula that reproduces their results as well as various exact limits with disgressions less than 1% (in particular, their formula incorporates the parametrization of the exchange energy by Perrot and Dharma-wardana [26]). We adopt a modification of this formula given by IIT [11].

The exchange-correlation free energy, fe​ef_{ee}, is obtained by integration from Eq. (11). It is important to note that Tanaka et al.[24] give a fit to the interaction energy of the electron fluid but not to the thermodynamic internal energy (the quantities differ at finite θ\theta). This enabled Tanaka et al. to obtain fe​ef_{ee} by integration of their fitting formula over Γe\Gamma_{e} at constant θ\theta (the integration of the internal energy would have to be performed at constant rsr_{s}). Note also that the results of IIT are nonrelativistic.

More recently, SB [22] proposed other parametrizations of the exchange and correlation free energies. At moderate rsr_{s}, comparison of the formulae given by SB and IIT reveals only small differences, which do not exceed the uncertainty in the various numerical results found in the literature[26, 27]. Unlike IIT, SB evaluated the exchange energy at θ<1\theta<1 in the relativistic case. On the other hand, the SB fit reaches the classical OCP limit at large rsr_{s} and moderate Γe\Gamma_{e} with disgressions up to 4.4%, while the parametrization of IIT is several times more accurate in this limit. We shall use the IIT’s formula hereafter.

VI Electron screening

VI.1 Numerical calculations

In order to calculate the screening contribution, we have employed the model of Ref.[8], outlined in Sect. II. The HNC equations were solved numerically for the effective screened interionic potential (9) to obtain fi​i+fi​ef_{ii}+f_{ie}, ui​i+ui​eu_{ii}+u_{ie}, and Pi​i+Pi​eP_{ii}+P_{ie}, and for the bare Coulomb potential to obtain fi​if_{ii}, ui​iu_{ii}, and Pi​iP_{ii}. The difference represents the screening (i​eie) contribution to the thermodynamic quantities.

The previous numerical results [8] have been obtained for the hydrogen plasma (Z=1Z=1). We extend the calculations to different values of ZZ and a larger set of rsr_{s}. Figure 2 shows the effective potentials VeffV^{\rm eff} for Z=6Z=6 and Z=26Z=26 at several values of rsr_{s}, compared with the bare Coulomb potential and with VeffV^{\rm eff} in the zero-temperature (θ=0\theta=0) RPA approximation (no local field correction). One can see that the latter approximation works well at the small value of rs=0.0256r_{s}=0.0256 (lower panels), while it breaks down completely at rs=1r_{s}=1 (upper panels).

The bulk of the calculations has been performed in the nonrelativistic approximation, for 13 ion charges from Z=1Z=1 to Z=26Z=26 listed in the first column of Table 2, at 10 values of the density parameter rsr_{s} ranging from rs=0.0256r_{s}=0.0256 to rs≈2r_{s}\approx 2, and, at each ZZ and rsr_{s}, for several tens of values of the coupling parameter Γi\Gamma_{i} which range from the DH limit at Γi=0.001\Gamma_{i}=0.001 to Γi∼200\Gamma_{i}\sim 200. As an example, calculated values of the normalized screening part of the free energy fi​ef_{ie} at Z=6Z=6 are shown by filled circles in Fig. 3. Note that it is the account of the finite electron temperature in the dielectric function that allows us to reach the correct TCP DH limit at low values of Γi\Gamma_{i} (see Ref.[8]).

In order to supplement the aforementioned nonrelativistic data at higher densities, we have also performed calculations using the Jancovici [12] zero-temperature dielectric function. The results are shown in Fig. 3 for Γi≥1\Gamma_{i}\geq 1 and rs=0.0625r_{s}=0.0625 (x=0.224x=0.224), 0.0256 (x=0.545x=0.545), and 0.008 (x=1.75x=1.75). A comparison for the case of rs=0.0625r_{s}=0.0625 confirms that the zero-temperature approximation works well at small rsr_{s} and large Γ\Gamma (where θ≪1\theta\ll 1 due to the relation (5)); this conclusion is corroborated by inspection of Fig. 2.

Thus the numerical results cover all values of rsr_{s} and Γ\Gamma (i.e., ρ\rho and TT) that are relevant for liquid EIPs. At rs≳1r_{s}\gtrsim 1 and Γi≳1\Gamma_{i}\gtrsim 1, the formation of bound states sets in. At rs≲10−2r_{s}\lesssim 10^{-2} and Γi≲1\Gamma_{i}\lesssim 1, the temperature reaches the values T≳3×107​Z5/3T\gtrsim 3\times 10^{7}Z^{5/3} K, where the electron screening effects are completely unimportant. Finally, at Γi≳170\Gamma_{i}\gtrsim 170, solidification takes place.

VI.2 Analytic formulae

The calculated values of the screening free energy are fitted by the following function of rsr_{s}, Γe\Gamma_{e}, and ZZ:

fi​e=−Γe​cD​H​Γe+cT​F​a​Γeν​g1​(rs)​h1​(x)1+[b​Γe+a​g2​(rs)​Γeν/rs]​h2​(x).f_{ie}=-\Gamma_{e}\,{c_{DH}\sqrt{\Gamma_{e}}+c_{TF}a\Gamma_{e}^{\nu}g_{1}(r_{s})h_{1}(x)\over 1+\left[b\,\sqrt{\Gamma_{e}}+ag_{2}(r_{s})\Gamma_{e}^{\nu}/r_{s}\right]h_{2}(x)}. (29)

The parameter

cD​H=Z3​[(1+Z)3/2−1−Z3/2]c_{DH}={Z\over\sqrt{3}}\left[(1+Z)^{3/2}-1-Z^{3/2}\right] (30)

The parameter c∞=(18/175)​(12/π)2/3=0.2513c_{\infty}=(18/175)(12/\pi)^{2/3}=0.2513 is consistent with the Thomas-Fermi approximation [28], which becomes exact at small rsr_{s} and very large ZZ (cf. Ref.[16]). The parameters

a\displaystyle a =\displaystyle= 1.11​Z0.475,\displaystyle 1.11\,Z^{0.475},
b\displaystyle b =\displaystyle= 0.2+0.078​(ln⁡Z)2,\displaystyle 0.2+0.078\,(\ln Z)^{2},
ν\displaystyle\nu =\displaystyle= 1.16+0.08​ln⁡Z\displaystyle 1.16+0.08\ln Z

provide a low-order approximation to fi​ef_{ie} (with a maximum error up to 30% at large ZZ and rs≳1r_{s}\gtrsim 1), while the functions

g1​(rs)\displaystyle g_{1}(r_{s}) =\displaystyle= 1+0.7821+Γe​(Z/rs)3​(ΓeZ)1/2,\displaystyle 1+{0.78\over 21+\Gamma_{e}(Z/r_{s})^{3}}\left({\Gamma_{e}\over Z}\right)^{1/2}, (32)
g2​(rs)\displaystyle g_{2}(r_{s}) =\displaystyle= 1+Z−19​(1+10.001​Z2+2​Γe)​rs31+6​rs2\displaystyle 1+{Z-1\over 9}\left(1+\frac{1}{0.001\,Z^{2}+2\Gamma_{e}}\right){r_{s}^{3}\over 1+6\,r_{s}^{2}} (33)

improve the fit at relatively large rsr_{s} and reduce the maximum fractional error in fi​ef_{ie} to 4.3%, and the root-mean-square (rms) error to ∼1.5\sim 1.5%.

The factors h1(x)=[1+(vF/c)6Z−1/3]−1h_{1}(x)=[1+(v_{F}/c)^{6}Z^{-1/3}]^{-1} (where vF=c​x/1+x2v_{F}=cx/\sqrt{1+x^{2}} is the electron Fermi velocity) and h2(x)=(1+x2)−1/2h_{2}(x)=(1+x^{2})^{-1/2} are relativistic corrections and may be omitted at x≪1x\ll 1.

Note that fi​ef_{ie} constitutes only a part of the ion excess free energy fi​i+fi​ef_{ii}+f_{ie}. The fit to this latter quantity is given by the sum of Eqs. (28) and (29). The second and third columns of Table 2 present the rms and maximum relative differences between the calculated and fitted values of fi​i+fi​ef_{ii}+f_{ie} at each value of ZZ. The comparison has been done for the set of finite-temperature numerical results at 0.1≤Γi≤1700.1\leq\Gamma_{i}\leq 170 and 0.0625≤rs≤2.0740.0625\leq r_{s}\leq 2.074. The remaining four columns of the table present the rms and maximum relative differences for the (i​i+i​eii+ie) internal energy and pressure, derived from the fits by the use of the thermodynamic relations

u=(∂f∂ln⁡Γ)rs,β​P/n=13​[u−(∂f∂ln⁡rs)Γ].u=\left(\partial f\over\partial\ln\Gamma\right)_{r_{s}},\qquad\beta P/n=\frac{1}{3}\left[u-\left(\partial f\over\partial\ln r_{s}\right)_{\Gamma}\right]. (34)

The bottom line of the table is given for reference and presents the difference between the fit (28) and numerical HNC data in the OCP model (i.e., without the i​eie contribution).

The calculated and fitted values of fi​ef_{ie} are shown in Fig. 3 for Z=6Z=6 and in Fig. 4 for Z=1,2Z=1,2, and 10. For comparison, we have plotted the fit of Yakovlev and Shalybkov [16] (YS) to their relativistic calculations, carried out in the zero-temperature approximation (justified at small rsr_{s} and large Γe\Gamma_{e}). In Fig. 4 we have also plotted fi​ef_{ie} given by an analytic expression of Ebeling et al.[29] reproduced by SB[22]. For the hydrogen plasma (Z=1Z=1) it reproduces the Padé approximations of Ref.[30]. One can see that the fit of YS, in the range of its validity, agrees with our results. On the contrary, the approximation of Refs.[29, 22] is clearly invalid in most cases. It exhibits unphysical behavior around Γi∼0.1\Gamma_{i}\sim 0.1, predicting an enhancement of screening with decreasing rsr_{s} (e. g., for Z=1Z=1 and Γi=0.1\Gamma_{i}=0.1 it gives larger fi​ef_{ie} at rs=0.41r_{s}=0.41 than at rs=1.464r_{s}=1.464). Moreover, the extrapolation to Z>1Z>1, proposed in Ref.[29], severely underestimates the screening effects.

Figure 5 exhibits an analogous comparison for the excess free energy (10), for Z=1Z=1. We have also plotted the Padé-approximation of IIT [11]. Although the disgressions between the fit and numerical data of Ref.[11] lie within 0.4%, there are significant deviations between the IIT fit and our present results. This discrepancy originates from the relatively small number of numerical calculations used by IIT (32 computed values at 0.1≤Γi≤100.1\leq\Gamma_{i}\leq 10 and 0.1≤θ≤100.1\leq\theta\leq 10). Our fit, based on a much larger set of numerical data, not only reproduces these data but also the numerical results of IIT [11].

The excess ionic pressure Pi​i+Pi​eP_{ii}+P_{ie} is shown in Fig. 6. Calculated data are compared with the pressure obtained by differentiation (34) of our fit and of SB fit. The DH approximation, shown for reference, is calculated as the difference between the DH pressures of the electron-ion TCP and the electron OCP. The importance of the screening effects is verified by comparison of our calculated and fitted pressure with the pressure of the OCP in the rigid background, Pi​iP_{ii}, also shown in the figure.

Figure 7 demonstrates the validity of the EOS derived from our analytic formulae. The EOS of the perfect ion-electron gas is compared with the EOS which includes the nonideality of the electron and ion fluids but neglects the i​eie interactions; solid lines show the complete EOS. The gaps in some isotherms indicate the regions where the formation of bound states could not be neglected. The significant deviations of the broken lines from the full lines in certain ranges of ρ\rho and TT demonstrate the importance of the ion-electron screening effects.

VII Multi-ionic mixtures

The multi-ionic mixture is a straightforward generalization of the previous single-ion model. In that case the effective Hamiltonian (8) reads :

Heff=Ki+12​V​∑𝐤≠04​π​e2k2​[ρZ​𝐤​ρZ​𝐤∗ϵ⁡(k)−Ni​⟨Z2⟩]H^{\rm eff}=K_{i}\,+\,\frac{1}{2V}\sum_{{\bf k}\neq 0}\frac{4\pi e^{2}}{k^{2}}\left[\frac{\rho_{Z\bf k}\rho_{Z\bf k}^{\ast}}{\epsilon(k)}-N_{i}\langle Z^{2}\rangle\right] (35)

where ρZ​𝐤=∑iZi​ρi​𝐤\rho_{Z\bf k}=\sum_{i}Z_{i}\rho_{i\bf k} are the Fourier components of the ion charge number fluctuations.

For the binary ionic mixture in a rigid electron background (ϵ⁡(k)=1​∀k\epsilon(k)=1\,\forall k), the excess (non-ideal) free energy of the mixture, as well as the related thermodynamic quantities, can be expressed with high accuracy by the so-called “linear mixing rule” (LMR) in terms of the free energy of the pure phases :

fex​(Z1,Z2,Γe,x1)≈x1​fex​(Γ1,x1=1)+(1−x1)​fex​(Γ2,x1=0),f_{\rm ex}(Z_{1},Z_{2},\Gamma_{e},x_{1})\approx x_{1}f_{\rm ex}(\Gamma_{1},x_{1}=1)+(1-x_{1})f_{\rm ex}(\Gamma_{2},x_{1}=0), (36)

where Γi=Γe​Zi5/3\Gamma_{i}=\Gamma_{e}Z_{i}^{5/3} and x1=N1/(N1+N2)x_{1}=N_{1}/(N_{1}+N_{2}). The very high level of accuracy of the LMR (36) was first demonstrated by Hansen et al.[21] and confirmed later on by several authors, using very accurate MC calculations (e.g., [5, 31]).

The validity of the LMR in the case of an ionic mixture immersed in a responsive finite-temperature electron background, as described by the Hamiltonian (35), has been examined by Hansen et al.[21] in the first-order thermodynamic perturbation approximation, and more recently by Chabrier and Ashcroft [32], who have solved the HNC equations with the effective screened potentials for arbitrary charge ratios ranging from a symmetric case (Z2/Z1∼1Z_{2}/Z_{1}\sim 1) to a highly asymmetric case (Z2/Z1≫1Z_{2}/Z_{1}\gg 1). These authors found that the LMR remains valid to a high degree of accuracy when the electron response is taken into account in the interionic potential, except possibly for highly asymmetric mixtures in the region of weak degeneracy of the electron gas (where the departure from linearity can reach a few percent).

VIII Conclusions

We have developed a completely analytic model for the free energy of fully ionized electron-ion Coulomb plasmas. The ideal part of the free energy of electrons and ions is described by Eqs. (12)–(15) and is accurately represented by the analytic fits given by Eqs. (18)–(24). Note that these formulae provide the thermodynamic quantities of a free electron gas for any degeneracy and relativity. For the excess free energy of the electron fluid at finite temperature, we adopt the analytic approximation from Ref.[11]. For the excess free energy of the classical ionic OCP, we provide a simple interpolation (28) which accurately reproduces the Monte Carlo results at Γi≥1\Gamma_{i}\geq 1 and the Debye-Hückel-Abe limit for Γi≪1\Gamma_{i}\ll 1. Finally, we have taken into account the ion-electron interactions by solving the hypernetted-chain equations for a large set of the parameters Γi\Gamma_{i}, rsr_{s}, and ZZ and constructed an analytic fit given by Eq. (29). Our analytic formulae reproduce fi​i+fi​ef_{ii}+f_{ie} with accuracy ∼1−2\sim 1-2%, and the derivatives of this function with respect to rsr_{s} and Γi\Gamma_{i} give an excess internal energy and pressure with relative errors not larger than a few percent. This analytic approximation is significantly more accurate than previous approximations of the free energy of the electron-ion plasmas.

As mentioned in the introduction, our calculations imply full ionization, i.e. point-like ions from which their bound electrons are stripped completely. This model is realistic in various conditions at high temperatures or densities encountered in modern laser experiments and in various astrophysical situations like, for example, stellar, brown dwarf and giant planet interiors, or the envelopes of neutron stars. In these situations, complete ionization can be safely assumed. Furthermore, the present model can be used as the basis of more elaborated equations of state aimed at describing the thermodynamic properties of partially ionized plasmas and ionization equilibrium. Work in this direction is in progress.
